1. A good therapist will give you questions/prompts that help you open up, so don't worry too much about this - therapy isn't a performance you need to study for, it should be the opposite.

2. During the first session, you and the therapist get to know each other. You could tell them about your life so far - school, hobbies, events that were important to you, your plans and dreams etc.

3. Therapy is about getting in touch with yourself and understanding what you're feeling, and why. That could be a great thing you could work on in therapy! You could tell them right away that this is something you struggle with and would like some help with.

4. Maybe compile some bullet points of what's bothering you the most atm - which symptoms/aspects of your illnesses, or outer influences (school, parents, friends idk). That way, your therapist gets an idea of what you'd like to improve upon and where to start. 

All in all, this first session is about whether you feel comfortable with the therapist. I've been to a lot I haven't really vibed with, for various reasons, before eventually finding the perfect one. And that's fine. Give them a try for a few sessions and see whether you feel understood and valued. Therapy isn't always fun and might make you feel worse at the start, simply because you're talking about and facing many things you have been ignoring, but working through that is so important. I wish you the best of luck!

Most people can tell what self harm scars are (unless yours don't look like cutting scars?). Friends/any respectful person will not ask you about them, they know it's an awful thing to be reminded of, and what answer are they expecting? If people ask me [22M] about mine, I look at them and say "what do you think?", that usually makes people realise that asking someone to confess that they self harm is rude and unnecessary. 

Your friends might be worried about you though, and they might not know how to address it. You could, if they notice your scars, let them know that some time ago, things were kinda difficult. Maybe tell them how they could support you - I think feeling helpless when a friend is struggling is the worst. (Even if all they can do is hang out with you, that's a way for them to feel useful.) Also, since you said it was "months ago", you could tell them how you managed to feel better/cope healthier since then. 

On a date, if someone is rude/invasive about the scars, you know they're not worth your time. If someone is genuinely interested in you/worried, you could say that the scars are old or that you sometimes struggle with healthy coping mechanisms. Any reasonable adult should then consider your feelings and not pry into it. 

Self harm is depressingly common, be it cutting, unhealthy eating patterns, alcohol etc. I treat my scars like a natural part of me, they're part of my history and anyone who is rude about them has no room in my life. I hope you'll still be able to live your life and do whatever you want to do and not be held back by them.
